Guidestar-Free Adaptive Optics with Asymmetric Apertures
problem Telescopes see blurry images when Earth's atmosphere warps light. Current fixing systems need a reference star or special sensors.
approach Use an oddly-shaped telescope opening and a learned system to read distortions directly from any scene, then bounce light to correct them live.
read the full first-principles story
the big picture

Telescopes and microscopes struggle to see clearly through turbulent air or cloudy glass — the atmosphere or optical imperfections scramble incoming light waves. We want to correct this distortion in real-time and in software, recovering sharp images of distant objects without needing artificial reference beacons (guidestars) placed in the sky.

why it's hard

Measuring how much the light has been distorted requires knowing either the original light pattern (which you don't have for natural scenes) or a bright reference star at a known position (which may not exist or be too faint). The trick is getting the wavefront measurement from the blurry image alone, using only the quirky shape of the telescope's opening.

the core idea

They use an asymmetric telescope pupil (an oddly-shaped opening instead of a circular one) that encodes wavefront distortions into measurable patterns in the image. Two neural networks then infer the optical distortion from these patterns and predict what the true image looks like. A deformable mirror at the pupil plane applies the computed correction optically, closing the loop in real-time.

why it works

An asymmetric pupil breaks the symmetry of how light spreads in the image, so the blurry pattern itself now contains information about the distortion — like a broken mirror shape tells you how light was bent. Neural networks learn this relationship from training data, so correcting distortions that haven't been seen before still works reasonably well.

the payoff

The system corrects optical aberrations without a guidestar, uses 100× fewer images, and needs 1000× less computation than older phase-retrieval methods. It enables sharp imaging of natural scenes through unknown obstacles (dust, haze, or fog) with only a camera and a controllable mirror.

Gabor Fields: Orientation-Selective Level-of-Detail for Volume Rendering
problem Rendering smooth clouds and fog efficiently requires different detail levels in different places, but current systems need retrained models at each level.
approach Use oriented frequency filters that skip unnecessary fine detail automatically, accelerating rendering without reprocessing or storing extra data.
read the full first-principles story
the big picture

Rendering complex 3D volumes (smoke, clouds, semi-transparent materials) is computationally expensive. To speed it up, we use hierarchies: show low detail far from the camera and high detail up close. This is easy with traditional voxel grids but hard with modern Gaussian-based representations, which are memory-efficient but don't have built-in levels of detail.

why it's hard

Gaussian representations avoid the memory cost of voxel grids, but constructing a hierarchical version is awkward: prefiltering bloats memory, recomputing each level is expensive, and smooth transitions between levels are hard to guarantee. You need a method that prunes or filters without refitting.

the core idea

Gabor Fields replace Gaussian elements with Gabor kernels (sinusoidal functions modulated by a Gaussian envelope) that naturally encode frequency and orientation. Rendering can select which frequencies to use at each viewing distance. Pruning high-frequency kernels automatically reduces detail without refitting or extra storage.

why it works

Gabor kernels inherently encode frequency information (spatial scale), so reducing detail is as simple as dropping the high-frequency components. This is cheap and automatic, unlike Gaussian prefiltering. Stochastically sampling different frequencies at different ray depths creates smooth transitions between hierarchy levels.

the payoff

Gabor Fields enable smooth, continuous level-of-detail for Gaussian volumes with no refitting, no extra memory, and faster rendering. Ray traversal accelerates because high-frequency components can be masked, allowing the renderer to skip large volumetric regions.

Component Modes Synthesis Method with Multiple Partitions for Large-scale Eigenvalue Problem
problem Computing how huge structures vibrate requires solving enormous math problems that are too heavy for one computer to handle alone.
approach Split the structure into overlapping regions, solve each piece separately from multiple angles, then blend the answers together smartly.
read the full first-principles story
the big picture

When engineers design structures like buildings, bridges, or aircraft, they need to simulate how the thing vibrates and moves when disturbed. This vibrational analysis is critical for safety and performance, but for large, complex structures, the math becomes so expensive that it can take days to compute on supercomputers.

why it's hard

The full problem is too large to solve in one go. Standard approaches divide the structure into smaller chunks (substructures) and solve each one independently, then stitch the results together. But the quality of the results depends on having a good basis—a set of mathematical building blocks—that captures all the important vibrational modes. When you use just the natural vibrations from each individual substructure, you don't get enough diversity to represent the full structure's behavior accurately, so you need many more modes than should theoretically be necessary.

the core idea

Instead of using vibration modes from just one partition of the structure, the researchers use modes from multiple overlapping partitions—like dividing a bridge into chunks in different ways and mining vibrations from each way separately. This gives a richer set of building blocks. They further speed things up by approximating the interfaces between chunks (the boundaries where pieces touch) using low-frequency signals derived from those modes, rather than keeping the full expensive representation at every interface.

why it works

Overlapping partitions expose more of the structure's natural patterns; each partition captures different aspects of how the thing wants to move. Using modes from many different partitions is like getting suggestions from many different people—you get a more complete picture. The low-frequency approximation at interfaces works because most of the important information lives in the big, slow vibrations, not the tiny, fast ones, so you can throw away the fast wiggles without losing much accuracy.

the payoff

The method improves accuracy by three orders of magnitude compared to standard Component Mode Synthesis, meaning you get the same answer using vastly fewer mathematical degrees of freedom. It also scales better on distributed supercomputers—communication and memory usage both improve—making large-scale simulations for film effects and industrial design far more practical.

Connecting the dots

One lifecycle, one shift

Lay the six stages end to end and the whole conference is a single pipeline: a thing is described, made to behave, lit to be seen, captured from reality, invented by the machine, and delivered to the world. Each stage exists because the one before it left something undone — a shape is nothing until it moves, motion is invisible until it's lit, and lighting a hand-built world is pointless if you could have captured or generated one instead.

And one change cuts across all six. The old craft of graphics was built from physics and geometry — equations for light, meshes for shape, simulations for motion. This year, a learned layer sits on top of every stage: the machine now helps describe shapes, predict motion, clean up lighting, fill in captured reality, and — most of all — invent new content outright. The single most-used tool across these 153 papers is the generative kind of model that a few years ago only made pictures.

Computer graphics has always been the craft of making a believable world by hand, one physical rule at a time. Its 2026 turn is the same craft learning to generate itself — geometry and physics still at the core, but a machine that increasingly describes, captures, and invents the world for us.
